name: Calendula extract

lead: Calendula extract comes from pot marigold flowers and is used in creams and balms to calm irritated skin so it looks less red and more comfortable. It has a long history in traditional wound-care products.

Laboratory studies report anti-inflammatory activity for flower extracts, though the mechanism in human skin is not established in the sources reviewed. A 2019 systematic review of calendula as a single wound-healing treatment covered 14 studies, 7 in animals and 7 clinical trials. No published trial listed here has tested it for appearance goals such as acne or skin aging.

paras: People use it in soothing creams, balms and toners applied to irritated or sensitive skin, usually as part of a gentle routine. It is typically one ingredient among several.
The sources reviewed do not describe significant adverse effects of topical use; safety data are limited to the small studies cited.

angle.text: Calendula extract is used to calm irritated skin so it looks less red and more even. Lab studies report anti-inflammatory activity, and human and animal studies have looked at wound healing.

lead: Calendula extract is a preparation from the flowers of Calendula officinalis (pot marigold), used in topical skincare and traditional wound-care products. People use calendula creams, oils and balms to soothe irritated, dry or sun-exposed skin and to support a calmer, healthier-looking complexion; the plant's oil is widely used in skin products.[1]

Laboratory studies have reported anti-inflammatory properties for flower extracts,[2] and human and animal studies have examined it mainly for wound healing.[3] A 2019 systematic review of calendula extract as a single treatment for wound healing covered 14 studies, 7 animal experiments and 7 clinical trials.[3] A small trial measured the skin's mechanical properties after a calendula cream was applied to the cheeks.[4]

In Europe, the EMA's herbal committee recognises calendula flower preparations for traditional use on minor skin inflammation such as sunburn, minor wounds, and mouth or throat inflammation, on the basis of long-standing use rather than clinical trials.[5]
infobox: Topical creams, oils, gels, mouthwash, teas
Triterpenoid esters, carotenoids, flavonol glycosides, saponins[1]
Traditional use for minor skin inflammation and wounds (HMPC)[5]

paras: Calendula extract and calendula oil appear in cosmetics and skin-care products; Wikipedia attributes this to the flowers' saponins, resins and essential oils and notes the oil is widely used in skin products.[1] One study applied a newly formulated calendula cream to cheeks and measured skin elasticity, fatigue and hydration with a cutometer, a device used to assess the effects of cosmetic and anti-ageing products.[4] Calendula also features in herbal soothing products for irritation-prone skin.

Ancient Greek, Roman, Middle Eastern and Indian cultures used the flowers as a medicinal herb and as a dye for fabrics, foods and cosmetics, and leaves were made into poultices for scratches and shallow cuts.[1] The EMA's HMPC monograph lists traditional use for minor skin inflammation such as sunburn, minor wounds, and minor mouth or throat inflammation, for people over 6 years (skin) or over 12 (mouth and throat), and advises consulting a doctor if symptoms last longer than a week.[5] Studies have also examined it in a mouthwash for radiation-induced oral mucositis.[6]

Petals and pollen contain triterpenoid esters and carotenoids such as flavoxanthin and auroxanthin, which give the yellow-orange colour. Flowers also contain flavonol glycosides, oleanane-type triterpene glycosides, saponins and a sesquiterpene glucoside.[1] In laboratory studies, extracts have shown possible antiviral, anti-genotoxic and anti-inflammatory effects, and methanol and ethanol extracts showed antibacterial and antifungal activity.[1]

A rodent study found that oral flower extract at 250 and 500 mg/kg reduced induced paw swelling by roughly 51 and 66 percent in one model, and it also reported effects in a chronic inflammation model.[2] A 1996 paper reported that an aqueous extract of the flowers induced vascularisation in an assay, an observation linked to proposed wound-healing effects.[7] A 2006 in vitro study of a laser-activated extract reported cytotoxic and lymphocyte-activating effects.[8]

The 2019 systematic review reported that, in acute wound healing, treated groups showed faster resolution of the inflammatory phase and increased granulation tissue.[3] In the 40-patient mouthwash trial, patients receiving a 2% calendula extract mouthwash were compared with 20 receiving placebo for radiation-induced oropharyngeal mucositis, with antioxidant capacity also examined.[6] The EMA committee noted that clinical studies in leg ulcers and burns had design problems that prevented firm conclusions.[5]

The EMA monograph states that skin sensitisation has been reported, with unknown frequency, and that the preparations are contraindicated in people hypersensitive to plants of the daisy family (Asteraceae).[5]

Newer work studies calendula as a component of delivery systems: solid lipid nanoparticles,[9] chitosan hydrogels loaded with silver nanoparticles and calendula extract,[10] polyacrylamide hydrogel bandages,[11] an alginate hydrogel with calendula glycolic extract tested on 50 rats over 28 days,[12] and a zinc-oxide nanoparticle cream tested on burns in rats.[13] A 2025 in vitro study reported on calendula extract and mortality of Demodex folliculorum mites, which are associated with some skin conditions.[14] A 2025 paper compared herbal wound-care creams, one containing calendula oil, with a placebo and a commercial cream.[15] These findings come from animal or cell models.

The 2019 systematic review included seven clinical trials of calendula extract for wound healing.[3] In a randomized study of 40 head-and-neck cancer patients, a 2% calendula mouthwash was compared with placebo for radiation-induced oropharyngeal mucositis.[6] A study of a calendula cream on mechanical parameters of human skin has also been published.[4] Trials focused on cosmetic skin appearance, such as acne or ageing, were not found.
